doi:10.1175/mwr-d-16-0417.1.title: The HARMONIE–AROME Model Configuration in the ALADIN–HIRLAM NWP System
doi:10.1175/mwr-d-16-0417.1.summary: The aim of this article is to describe the reference configuration of the convection-permitting numerical weather prediction (NWP) model HARMONIE-AROME, which is used for operational short-range weather forecasts in Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, and Sweden. It is developed, maintained, and validated as part of the shared ALADIN–HIRLAM system by a collaboration of 26 countries in Europe and northern Africa on short-range mesoscale NWP. HARMONIE–AROME is based on the model AROME developed within the ALADIN consortium. Along with the joint modeling framework, AROME was implemented and utilized in both northern and southern European conditions by the above listed countries, and this activity has led to extensive updates to the model’s physical parameterizations. In this paper the authors present the differences in model dynamics and physical parameterizations compared with AROME, as well as important configuration choices of the reference, such as lateral boundary conditions, model levels, horizontal resolution, model time step, as well as topography, physiography, and aerosol databases used. Separate documentation will be provided for the atmospheric and surface data-assimilation algorithms and observation types used, as well as a separate description of the ensemble prediction system based on HARMONIE–AROME, which is called HarmonEPS.

doi:10.1175/2011mwr3623.1.title: Assimilation of Surface-Based Boundary Layer Profiler Observations during a Cool-Season Weather Event Using an Observing System Simulation Experiment. Part II: Forecast Assessment
doi:10.1175/2011mwr3623.1.summary: In this study, atmospheric analyses obtained through assimilation of temperature, water vapor, and wind profiles from a potential network of ground-based remote sensing boundary layer profiling instruments were used to generate short-range ensemble forecasts for each assimilation experiment performed in Part I. Remote sensing systems evaluated during this study include the Doppler wind lidar (DWL), Raman lidar (RAM), microwave radiometer (MWR), and the Atmospheric Emitted Radiance Interferometer (AERI). Overall, the results show that the most accurate forecasts were achieved when mass (temperature and humidity profiles from the RAM, MWR, and/or AERI) and momentum (wind profiles from the DWL) observations were assimilated simultaneously, which is consistent with the main conclusion from Part I. For instance, the improved wind and moisture analyses obtained through assimilation of these observations contributed to more accurate forecasts of moisture flux convergence and the intensity and location of accumulated precipitation (ACPC) due to improved dynamical forcing and mesoscale boundary layer thermodynamic structure. An object-based verification tool was also used to assess the skill of the ACPC forecasts. Overall, total interest values for ACPC matched objects, along with traditional forecast skill statistics like the equitable threat score and critical success index, were most improved in the multisensor assimilation cases.

doi:10.1175/waf-d-17-0010.1.title: Storm-Based Probabilistic Hail Forecasting with Machine Learning Applied to Convection-Allowing Ensembles
doi:10.1175/waf-d-17-0010.1.summary: Forecasting severe hail accurately requires predicting how well atmospheric conditions support the development of thunderstorms, the growth of large hail, and the minimal loss of hail mass to melting before reaching the surface. Existing hail forecasting techniques incorporate information about these processes from proximity soundings and numerical weather prediction models, but they make many simplifying assumptions, are sensitive to differences in numerical model configuration, and are often not calibrated to observations. In this paper a storm-based probabilistic machine learning hail forecasting method is developed to overcome the deficiencies of existing methods. An object identification and tracking algorithm locates potential hailstorms in convection-allowing model output and gridded radar data. Forecast storms are matched with observed storms to determine hail occurrence and the parameters of the radar-estimated hail size distribution. The database of forecast storms contains information about storm properties and the conditions of the prestorm environment. Machine learning models are used to synthesize that information to predict the probability of a storm producing hail and the radar-estimated hail size distribution parameters for each forecast storm. Forecasts from the machine learning models are produced using two convection-allowing ensemble systems and the results are compared to other hail forecasting methods. The machine learning forecasts have a higher critical success index (CSI) at most probability thresholds and greater reliability for predicting both severe and significant hail.

doi:10.1175/waf-d-14-00105.1.title: A Review of Planetary Boundary Layer Parameterization Schemes and Their Sensitivity in Simulating Southeastern U.S. Cold Season Severe Weather Environments
doi:10.1175/waf-d-14-00105.1.summary: The representation of turbulent mixing within the lower troposphere is needed to accurately portray the vertical thermodynamic and kinematic profiles of the atmosphere in mesoscale model forecasts. For mesoscale models, turbulence is mostly a subgrid-scale process, but its presence in the planetary boundary layer (PBL) can directly modulate a simulation’s depiction of mass fields relevant for forecast problems. The primary goal of this work is to review the various parameterization schemes that the Weather Research and Forecasting Model employs in its depiction of turbulent mixing (PBL schemes) in general, and is followed by an application to a severe weather environment. Each scheme represents mixing on a local and/or nonlocal basis. Local schemes only consider immediately adjacent vertical levels in the model, whereas nonlocal schemes can consider a deeper layer covering multiple levels in representing the effects of vertical mixing through the PBL. As an application, a pair of cold season severe weather events that occurred in the southeastern United States are examined. Such cases highlight the ambiguities of classically defined PBL schemes in a cold season severe weather environment, though characteristics of the PBL schemes are apparent in this case. Low-level lapse rates and storm-relative helicity are typically steeper and slightly smaller for nonlocal than local schemes, respectively. Nonlocal mixing is necessary to more accurately forecast the lower-tropospheric lapse rates within the warm sector of these events. While all schemes yield overestimations of mixed-layer convective available potential energy (MLCAPE), nonlocal schemes more strongly overestimate MLCAPE than do local schemes.

doi:10.1002/qj.4765.title: Assessing the role of boreal summer intraseasonal oscillation on the severe heatwave of May 2015 over India
doi:10.1002/qj.4765.summary: In May 2015, the southeastern coastal states of India encountered one of the deadliest heatwaves in Indian history. Researchers have extensively studied the event to understand the underlying mechanisms and concluded that horizontal warm‐air advection from northwestern parts of India and adiabatic heating were the main attributing factors for the event. However, the large‐scale atmospheric processes that led to these conditions have not been thoroughly explored. In the present study, we show that this event was largely associated with the boreal summer intraseasonal oscillation (BSISO) that is prominent during this season. Our analysis shows that the BSISO dry phase lead to a persistent high‐pressure system, with anomalous subsidence favoring adiabatic heating and anticyclonic circulation anomalies increasing the northwesterly warm‐air advection. It is shown that a 55% to 75% contribution to the maximum surface air temperature (SAT) anomalies during the heatwave period can be attributed to BSISO‐related temperature anomalies. Furthermore, the results show that, in the absence of BSISO, the heat event would have dissipated with 1–2 hot days with much less intensity and the presence of the BSISO dry phase extended the heatwave duration by six days. The impact of BSISO on this heatwave was further substantiated by sensitivity experiments using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model. This analysis emphasizes that improving the forecasting skills of BSISO may facilitate the subseasonal forecast of local heatwave events.

doi:10.1017/eds.2023.7.title: Sinh-arcsinh-normal distributions to add uncertainty to neural network regression tasks: Applications to tropical cyclone intensity forecasts
doi:10.1017/eds.2023.7.summary: A simple method for adding uncertainty to neural network regression tasks in earth science via estimation of a general probability distribution is described. Specifically, we highlight the sinh-arcsinh-normal distributions as particularly well suited for neural network uncertainty estimation. The methodology supports estimation of heteroscedastic, asymmetric uncertainties by a simple modification of the network output and loss function. Method performance is demonstrated by predicting tropical cyclone intensity forecast uncertainty and by comparing two other common methods for neural network uncertainty quantification (i.e., Bayesian neural networks and Monte Carlo dropout). The simple approach described here is intuitive and applicable when no prior exists and one just wishes to parameterize the output and its uncertainty according to some previously defined family of distributions. The authors believe it will become a powerful, go-to method moving forward.

doi:10.1017/eds.2026.10045.title: Future wildfire risk in Southern Europe under changing land use, population, and climate: a data-driven approach
doi:10.1017/eds.2026.10045.summary: Wildfires are one of the most devastating natural disasters with wide impacts across economic sectors and society in Europe. It is, however, unclear how wildfire risk will evolve in the future under different climate scenarios, as it depends on future climate change scenarios as well as on land use and population changes. The aim of the study is to study end-of-century wildfire risk in Southern Europe, under different Shared Socioeconomic Pathways. A data-driven model is trained using historical data and a combination of other data sources representing hydro-meteorological variables, land cover, human activities, and topography. The best-performing model is the XGBoost model with an AUC of 0.93 and F1 score of 0.85. Using SHapley Additive exPlanations values, we identify the most influential predictors. The trained model is run daily using future climate projections from the Canadian Regional Climate Model version 5 under the SSP1–2.6 and SSP3–7.0 scenarios, including explicit changes in population and land cover. Future projections confirm that the wildfire risk will increase by the end of the century (2081–2100) in the SSP3–7.0, with limited changes in the SSP1–2.6 scenario. The results further show that including future land cover and population changes modulates the projected wildfire risk in scenario-dependent ways, highlighting the need to jointly account for climatic and socio-environmental drivers when assessing future wildfire risk.

doi:10.1017/eds.2022.8.title: Predicting spatiotemporal variability in radial tree growth at the continental scale with machine learning
doi:10.1017/eds.2022.8.summary: Tree-ring chronologies encode interannual variability in forest growth rates over long time periods from decades to centuries or even millennia. However, each chronology is a highly localized measurement describing conditions at specific sites where wood samples have been collected. The question whether these local growth variabilites are representative for large geographical regions remains an open issue. To overcome the limitations of interpreting a sparse network of sites, we propose an upscaling approach for annual tree-ring indices that approximate forest growth variability and compute gridded data products that generalize the available information for multiple tree genera. Using regression approaches from machine learning, we predict tree-ring indices in space and time based on climate variables, but considering also species range maps as constraints for the upscaling. We compare various prediction strategies in cross-validation experiments to identify the best performing setup. Our estimated maps of tree-ring indices are the first data products that provide a dense view on forest growth variability at the continental level with 0.5° and 0.0083° spatial resolution covering the years 1902–2013. Furthermore, we find that different genera show very variable spatial patterns of anomalies. We have selected Europe as study region and focused on the six most prominent tree genera, but our approach is very generic and can easily be applied elsewhere. Overall, the study shows perspectives but also limitations for reconstructing spatiotemporal dynamics of complex biological processes. The data products are available at https://www.doi.org/10.17871/BACI.248 .

arxiv:2611.30868.title: MUNDO: a multiresolution generative framework for temporal downscaling
arxiv:2611.30868.summary: Dynamical systems are often observed at coarse temporal resolution through sparse states or temporal aggregates, leaving the underlying fine-scale trajectories unresolved. Recovering these trajectories requires probabilistic models that capture the unresolved variability while remaining consistent with the observations. We present MUNDO (Multiresolution UNified DOwnscaling), a generative framework for temporal downscaling under general linear observation operators. MUNDO introduces a null-space parameterization that enforces exact observation consistency in a single network evaluation, unifying temporal interpolation and disaggregation. To capture complex multiscale dynamics, we leverage reverse Markov learning to factorize the observation operator into a hierarchy of successive coarsenings. Each level models only the degrees of freedom lost between adjacent resolutions. We evaluate MUNDO on two-scale Lorenz-96, four two-dimensional physical systems, and multivariate ERA5 reanalysis over Europe, for both temporal interpolation and disaggregation. Across datasets and tasks, MUNDO generally outperforms flow-based baselines. Single-step MUNDO achieves strong predictive skill, while recursive MUNDO generally improves temporal realism and ensemble calibration, with better spread-skill agreement and predictive coverage.

arxiv:2611.13359.title: Reconstructing Boundary Layer Wind Profiles with Machine Learning: A Comparative Study on IGRA Radiosonde Data
arxiv:2611.13359.summary: Wind profiles in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) drive short-range forecasting and wind-energy siting, yet sparse radiosonde coverage forces practitioners to interpolate them from a handful of physical predictors. We benchmark modern tabular learners against analytical parameterizations on 158,097 IGRA soundings. CatBoost, TabM, and FT-Transformer reduce RMSE to 1.3-1.6 m/s, against approximately 3 m/s for power-law and Monin-Obukhov fits; once the predictor set is fixed the three architectures differ by less than 0.05 m/s, so accuracy is driven by predictors rather than architecture. A cohort analysis of within-bin profile dispersion places an empirical floor of approximately 1.77 m/s on any point-wise predictor that uses standard radiosonde features, consistent with prior eddy-viscosity inversions. A one-dimensional Fourier Neural Operator applied as a post-hoc corrector to frozen tabular predictions reduces near-surface RMSE on U.S. stations from 1.5 to 1.2 m/s, while leaving upper-layer error unchanged. Further gains should come from new predictors rather than larger models.

arxiv:2611.07094.title: A Deep-Learning Framework for the Generalized Emulation of Atmospheric Radiative Transfer at Microwave Frequencies
arxiv:2611.07094.summary: This paper presents an application of machine learning to the problem of the computational expense of atmospheric radiative transfer calculations from physics-based models. While in recent studies individual emulators have been created that emulate certain radiative transfer schemes for different sensors, we show that a general framework can be applied to emulate the radiative transfer method itself. A fully connected deep neural network has been trained to predict top-of-atmosphere microwave radiances in all-sky conditions over various land, ocean and sea ice surfaces at all frequencies from 1 to 300 GHz, and for all incidence angles from 0 to 65 degrees. The reference models against which the emulator has been trained include an Eddington two-stream radiative transfer model for one-dimensional and pseudo-three-dimensional microwave brightness temperature simulations. This neural network architecture has also been separately trained to reproduce the explicit calculations of the Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM) for a single microwave imager. In all cases, the model architecture is successfully able predict microwave brightness temperatures by being trained directly on the optical properties of the atmosphere and surface and therefore directly emulating the radiative transfer method. Compared to the explicit schemes used to produce the training data, the GPU-enabled emulator is able to produce brightness temperature simulations more than three orders of magnitude faster and with a root-mean-squared-error less than 0.0348 K, 0.0531 K, and 0.0246 K against the independent test data for the two Eddington models and CRTM, respectively. Additionally, preliminary training using a full 3D Monte Carlo scheme for high-resolution simulations shows promising results for the application of this method to "exact" radiative transfer methods, and these results are discussed in Section IV.

arxiv:2611.17878.title: DySENSE: Dynamic Spatiotemporal ENergy Synthesis and Emulation with Satellite Imagery
arxiv:2611.17878.summary: Cities account for over two-thirds of the world's energy and more than 70% of global carbon dioxide emissions. City energy is essential for achieving the 2050 net-zero target and the UN's Sustainable Development Goals 7 and 11. Although existing studies have made progress, they are limited by data and methodological gaps. Existing studies are largely predictive for existing cities rather than generative for future cities; fine-grained, aligned monthly dynamic energy data are scarce; and existing GenAI models struggle to generate dynamic urban functional monthly energy. We present DySENSE, a joint multimodal GenAI framework that synthesizes static urban satellite imagery together with spatially aligned, dynamic monthly building energy consumption maps. We decouple long-term static urban morphology from short-term dynamic energy consumption. By conditioning on static urban land use, DySENSE can generate realistic, diverse and new static urban imagery with aligned energy maps. By conditioning on dynamic monthly and climate prompts, DySENSE can jointly generate dynamic, monthly energy consumption maps while keeping the urban morphology static. Experiments across four cities (New York, Washington, Norfolk, Busan) demonstrated that DySENSE can generate annotated high-fidelity synthetic energy data using less than 25% labelled data, boosting downstream prediction performance by 8% mIoU, and achieving strong energy dynamic consistency. Compared to existing methods, DySENSE significantly improved prediction performance (8.7% accuracy) and reduced prediction error (9%-18% CVRMSE, ASHRAE). DySENSE offers an effective foundation for energy-efficient cities, peak-load analysis, building performance simulation and dynamic demand response for city, energy, and building science. The data and code: https://huggingface.co/datasets/skl24/MUSE2 and https://github.com/kailaisun/DySENSE

doi:10.5194/gmd-14-2057-2021.title: HIDRA 1.0: deep-learning-based ensemble sea level forecasting in the northern Adriatic
doi:10.5194/gmd-14-2057-2021.summary: Interactions between atmospheric forcing, topographic constraints to air and water flow, and resonant character of the basin make sea level modelling in the Adriatic a challenging problem. In this study we present an ensemble deep-neural-network-based sea level forecasting method HIDRA, which outperforms our set-up of the general ocean circulation model ensemble (NEMO v3.6) for all forecast lead times and at a minuscule fraction of the numerical cost (order of 2×10-6). HIDRA exhibits larger bias but lower RMSE than our set-up of NEMO over most of the residual sea level bins. It introduces a trainable atmospheric spatial encoder and employs fusion of atmospheric and sea level features into a self-contained network which enables discriminative feature learning. HIDRA architecture building blocks are experimentally analysed in detail and compared to alternative approaches. Results show the importance of sea level input for forecast lead times below 24 h and the importance of atmospheric input for longer lead times. The best performance is achieved by considering the input as the total sea level, split into disjoint sets of tidal and residual signals. This enables HIDRA to optimize the prediction fidelity with respect to atmospheric forcing while compensating for the errors in the tidal model. HIDRA is trained and analysed on a 10-year (2006–2016) time series of atmospheric surface fields from a single member of ECMWF atmospheric ensemble. In the testing phase, both HIDRA and NEMO ensemble systems are forced by the ECMWF atmospheric ensemble. Their performance is evaluated on a 1-year (2019) hourly time series from a tide gauge in Koper (Slovenia). Spectral and continuous wavelet analysis of the forecasts at the semi-diurnal frequency (12 h) −1 and at the ground-state basin seiche frequency (21.5 h) −1 is performed. The energy at the basin seiche in the HIDRA forecast is close to that observed, while our set-up of NEMO underestimates it. Analyses of the January 2015 and November 2019 storm surges indicate that HIDRA has learned to mimic the timing and amplitude of basin seiches.

doi:10.5194/gmd-16-6247-2023.title: A robust error correction method for numerical weather prediction wind speed based on Bayesian optimization, variational mode decomposition, principal component analysis, and random forest: VMD-PCA-RF (version 1.0.0)
doi:10.5194/gmd-16-6247-2023.summary: Accurate wind speed prediction is crucial for the safe and efficient utilization of wind resources. However, current single-value deterministic numerical weather prediction methods employed by wind farms do not adequately meet the actual needs of power grid dispatching. In this study, we propose a new hybrid forecasting method for correcting 10 m wind speed predictions made by the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model. Our approach incorporates variational mode decomposition (VMD), principal component analysis (PCA), and five artificial intelligence algorithms: deep belief network (DBN), multilayer perceptron (MLP), random forest (RF), eXtreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), light gradient boosting machine (lightGBM), and the Bayesian optimization algorithm (BOA). We first predict wind speeds using the WRF model, with initial and lateral boundary conditions from the Global Forecast System (GFS). We then perform two sets of experiments with different input factors and apply BOA optimization to tune the four artificial intelligence models, ultimately building the final models. Furthermore, we compare the aforementioned five optimal artificial intelligence models suitable for five provinces in southern China in the wintertime: VMD-PCA-RF in December 2021 and VMD-PCA-lightGBM in January 2022. We find that the VMD-PCA-RF evaluation indices exhibit relative stability over nearly a year: the correlation coefficient (R) is above 0.6, forecasting accuracy (FA) is above 85 %, mean absolute error (MAE) is below 0.6 m s−1, root mean square error (RMSE) is below 0.8 m s−1, relative mean absolute error (rMAE) is below 60 %, and relative root mean square error (rRMSE) is below 75 %. Thus, for its promising performance and excellent year-round robustness, we recommend adopting the proposed VMD-PCA-RF method for improved wind speed prediction in models.

doi:10.1175/aies-d-24-0083.1.title: Measuring Sharpness of AI-Generated Meteorological Imagery
doi:10.1175/aies-d-24-0083.1.summary: AI-based algorithms are emerging in many meteorological applications that produce imagery as output, including for global weather forecasting models. However, the imagery produced by AI algorithms, especially by convolutional neural networks (CNNs), is often described as too blurry to look realistic, partly because CNNs tend to represent uncertainty as blurriness. This blurriness can be undesirable since it might obscure important meteorological features. More complex AI models, such as Generative AI models, produce images that appear to be sharper. However, improved sharpness may come at the expense of a decline in other performance criteria, such as standard forecast verification metrics. To navigate any trade-off between sharpness and other performance metrics it is important to quantitatively assess those other metrics along with sharpness. While there is a rich set of forecast verification metrics available for meteorological images, none of them focus on sharpness. This paper seeks to fill this gap by 1) exploring a variety of sharpness metrics from other fields, 2) evaluating properties of these metrics, 3) proposing the new concept of Gaussian Blur Equivalence as a tool for their uniform interpretation, and 4) demonstrating their use for sample meteorological applications, including a CNN that emulates radar imagery from satellite imagery (GREMLIN) and an AI-based global weather forecasting model (GraphCast).

doi:10.1175/aies-d-24-0085.1.title: An Operations-Based Evaluation of Tropical Cyclone Track and Intensity Forecasts from Artificial Intelligence Weather Prediction Models
doi:10.1175/aies-d-24-0085.1.summary: In just the past few years, multiple data-driven Artificial Intelligence Weather Prediction (AIWP) models have been developed. NHC verification procedures are used to evaluate 7-day track and intensity predictions for Northern Hemisphere tropical cyclones (TCs) from May to November 2023. Four open-source AIWP models initialized 4 times per day with GFS initial conditions are considered (FourCastNetv1, FourCastNetv2-small, GraphCast-operational, and Pangu-Weather). The AIWP track forecast errors and detection rates are comparable to those from the best-performing operational forecast models. However, the AIWP intensity forecast errors are larger than those of even the simplest intensity forecasts based on climatology and persistence. The AIWP models almost always reduce the TC intensity resulting in a substantial low bias. An idealized Rankine vortex was used to illustrate how minimizing RMS errors in the AIWP models contributes to this bias. The contribution of the AIWP models to the NHC model consensus was also evaluated. For track, adding the AIWP models improves the consensus by up to 11% at the longer time periods. This represents more than a 5-yr gain in accuracy based on the historical track forecast improvement of about 2% yr −1 . In contrast, the AIWP models did not improve the intensity consensus. A preliminary evaluation of the impact of the AIWP model initial conditions was performed by comparing forecasts initialized with GFS and ECMWF-Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) initial conditions for Northern Hemisphere cases in 2022–23. With the ECMWF-IFS initial conditions, the AIWP track forecasts significantly improved, but there was little improvement in the intensity forecasts. Significance Statement Weather prediction (WP) models based on artificial intelligence (AI) have proliferated over just the past few years. Once trained, these models run very quickly, making them appealing for operational forecasting. This study is one of the first to apply operational verification procedures to multiple open-source AIWP models to determine their applicability for operational forecasting. The track forecast errors are found to be comparable to those from the best operational models. However, the intensity forecasts have no skill relative to the simplest statistical models, due to a substantial low bias. Thus, the tropical cyclone (TC) track forecasts can be used directly as guidance, but postprocessing bias corrections or AIWP model architecture and training data modifications may be needed for useful TC intensity forecasts.

doi:10.1175/aies-d-23-0041.1.title: Transformer-Based Nowcasting of Radar Composites from Satellite Images for Severe Weather
doi:10.1175/aies-d-23-0041.1.summary: Weather radar data are critical for nowcasting and an integral component of numerical weather prediction models. While weather radar data provide valuable information at high resolution, their ground-based nature limits their availability, which impedes large-scale applications. In contrast, meteorological satellites cover larger domains but with coarser resolution. However, with the rapid advancements in data-driven methodologies and modern sensors aboard geostationary satellites, new opportunities are emerging to bridge the gap between ground- and space-based observations, ultimately leading to more skillful weather prediction with high accuracy. Here, we present a transformer-based model for nowcasting ground-based radar image sequences using satellite data up to 2-h lead time. Trained on a dataset reflecting severe weather conditions, the model predicts radar fields occurring under different weather phenomena and shows robustness against rapidly growing/decaying fields and complex field structures. Model interpretation reveals that the infrared channel centered at 10.3 μ m (C13) contains skillful information for all weather conditions, while lightning data have the highest relative feature importance in severe weather conditions, particularly in shorter lead times. The model can support precipitation nowcasting across large domains without an explicit need for radar towers, enhance numerical weather prediction and hydrological models, and provide radar proxy for data-scarce regions. Moreover, the open-source framework facilitates progress toward operational data-driven nowcasting. Significance Statement Ground-based weather radar data are essential for nowcasting, but data availability limitations hamper usage of radar data across large domains. We present a machine learning model, rooted in transformer architecture, that performs nowcasting of radar data using high-resolution geostationary satellite retrievals, for lead times of up to 2 h. Our model captures the spatiotemporal dynamics of radar fields from satellite data and offers accurate forecasts. Analysis indicates that the infrared channel centered at 10.3 μ m provides useful information for nowcasting radar fields under various weather conditions. However, lightning activity exhibits the highest forecasting skill for severe weather at short lead times. Our findings show the potential of transformer-based models for nowcasting severe weather.

doi:10.1029/2026ms005891.title: Mitigating Non‐Stationarity in Machine Learning–Based Downscaling of Climate Projections
doi:10.1029/2026ms005891.summary: Machine learning (ML) models perform well for climate downscaling when training and testing data follow similar statistical distributions. However, their performance can degrade as future climate statistics depart from the historical training record. We systematically investigate this problem by downscaling global temperature and precipitation fields across multiple emission pathways and two solar radiation modification (SRM) scenarios in the Max Planck Institute Earth System Model, comparing four machine learning configurations with bilinear interpolation and quantile delta mapping (QDM). A baseline ML model trained on the historical period degrades substantially under future forcing, reaching a global mean temperature error of 1.6 ° ${}^{\circ}$ C by 2100 under SSP5‐8.5. Preprocessing the ML model's input and target to reduce non‐stationarity via detrending and residual correction keeps the global mean error within 0.2 ° ${}^{\circ}$ C, comparable to that of QDM. All downscaling methods compared here show substantially lower skill when evaluated on anomalies rather than total fields, suggesting that much of their skill comes from correcting the climatological mean. QDM better preserves precipitation extremes and fine‐scale variance, whereas the ML models have lower pointwise errors. Downscaling the SRM scenarios produces larger spatial temperature biases than the emission pathways. We also generate 0.25 ° ${}^{\circ}$ monthly temperature projections for G6sulfur, providing a benchmark for future regional downscaling studies.

doi:10.1109/tgrs.2026.3745848.title: Spatiotemporal Forecasting of All-Weather Large-Scale Precipitable Water Vapor by Synergizing FY-4B AGRI, Ground-Based GNSS, and NWP Data
doi:10.1109/tgrs.2026.3745848.summary: Accurate forecasting of precipitable water vapor (PWV) is critical for weather prediction and hydrometeorological monitoring. Current PWV forecasting approaches suffer from limited accuracy and robustness, while their spatiotemporal (ST) resolutions are inherently constrained by reliance on single-source observations. This study presents a PWV retrieval strategy for the Fengyun-4B advanced geosynchronous radiation imager (AGRI) integrating K-means clustering and light gradient boosting machine (KLGBM), upon which a novel ST deep learning framework is developed for PWV forecast network (PFnet). Two recurrent variants, PFnet_TG and PFnet_PR, are proposed to synergistically fuse AGRI-retrieved PWV, GNSS-derived PWV, and GFS background fields, enabling all-weather PWV forecasting across Australia at 4-km spatial resolution, 15-min temporal resolution, and lead times of up to 6 h. Validations against independent GNSS PWV show that AGRI PWV retrieved by the KLGBM algorithm achieves an rms of 1.61 mm, representing improvements of 5.8%–31.8% over benchmark machine learning (ML) approaches. Independent ST evaluation demonstrates that PFnet_TG and PFnet_PR produce near-unbiased PWV forecasts, with rms values of 1.86 and 1.89 mm and PCC values of 0.98 and 0.97, respectively, corresponding to accuracy improvements of 25.3%–29.3% and 24.1%–28.1% over GraphCast, Pangu, and GFS. The incorporation of high-frequency AGRI and GNSS observations substantially reduces systematic biases in GFS PWV forecasts, lowering rms values to below 2 mm across the climatically transitional regions of southeastern Australia while maintaining an overall rms of approximately 2.2 mm at lead times exceeding 5 h. Across grassland regions, PFnet outperforms GraphCast, Pangu, and GFS by 16.5%–31.9% under varying weather conditions. Furthermore, PFnet-derived PWV forecasts exhibit stronger spatial correspondence with ERA5 integrated vapor transport (IVT) and greater spatial overlap with observed precipitation patterns, with intersection over union (IoU) scores exceeding those of GraphCast, Pangu, and GFS by 0.02–0.08. These findings highlight the value of heterogeneous-observation integration for fine-resolution PWV forecasting and its potential applications in severe-weather early warning.

doi:10.1088/2515-7620/aebfea.title: Direction-aware multiscale terrain fusion for 10 m wind forecast downscaling over Xinjiang, China
doi:10.1088/2515-7620/aebfea.summary: High-resolution near-surface winds are critical for wind-resource assessment, atmospheric transport modelling, and weather-risk management. However, global numerical weather prediction models do not adequately resolve fine-scale wind variability over complex terrain. We propose a direction-aware multi-scale terrain fusion U-Net (DMTF-UNet) to downscale 0.25° global forecast system 10 m wind forecasts to the 0.1° ERA5-Land grid over Xinjiang, China. A single model predicts the horizontal wind components at seven forecast lead times from 24 to 168 h. DMTF-UNet applies direction-preserving wind normalization and persistently fuses elevation and terrain-gradient information across multiple network scales. A vector-aware loss jointly constrains wind components, speed, and direction. Evaluation used a temporally independent 2024–2025 test set, with bilinear interpolation followed by linear regression and a conventional U-Net as benchmarks. All methods used common wind predictors and the same evaluation protocol. Across three independent training runs, DMTF-UNet achieved a mean wind-speed root-mean-square error of 1.013 m s−1 and wind-direction mean angular error of 26.41°. This represented a 10.5% reduction in wind-speed error relative to U-Net. DMTF-UNet outperformed both benchmarks at all seven leads, with statistically significant reductions in wind-speed and direction errors relative to U-Net. Spatial error maps showed marked wind-speed improvements in the Tarim Basin–southern Tianshan region, with widespread but spatially heterogeneous and lead-dependent directional gains. These findings support terrain-informed, vector-aware learning for deterministic near-surface wind downscaling over complex terrain.

doi:10.62201/tknpyy41.title: LSTM-Based Regional Sea Surface Temperature Prediction Model for Climate Projection in North Maluku
doi:10.62201/tknpyy41.summary: North Maluku Province, as an archipelagic region, is highly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, particularly the increasing frequency of extreme precipitation events, while facing limitations in observational data. This study aims to develop a regional sea surface temperature (SST) prediction model using a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to generate more accurate SST projections by applying bias correction to outputs from the BNU-ESM global climate model. doi:10.3390/jimaging12110568.title: Improving Instantaneous Rainfall Estimation from MSG Imagery with a Soft-Weighted Dual U-Net–XGBoost Strategy
doi:10.3390/jimaging12110568.summary: This study aims to improve quantitative precipitation estimation at high spatial and temporal resolutions using Meteosat Second Generation (MSG) satellite imagery. In this context, two complementary models are exploited for the classification of precipitation intensities into five classes, namely: No rain, Light rain, Moderate rain, Heavy rain and Very heavy rain. To better exploit the information, XGBoost captures the radiometric response at the individual pixel level, while U-Net extracts the texture and spatial context of the cloud neighborhood. The classification architecture merges the probabilistic responses derived from spectral signatures via XGBoost with the extraction of cloud spatio-textural features from the deep multiclass U-Net network. Their output probabilities are combined and recalibrated using a logistic regression meta-classifier into a unified probability vector. To obtain instantaneous estimates, the final value corresponds to the sum of the previously defined precipitation intensities, each multiplied by the probability predicted by the meta-classifier. The models are trained on ground radar observations and validated against temporally independent radar test events from Sétif. Instantaneous precipitation estimates, as well as accumulations, were calculated. The proposed hybrid model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art benchmark architectures (notably, MCM, Ada/Bag-ANN, and DST-ANN/SVM/RF). At the instantaneous scale, the model achieves remarkable accuracy, with a correlation coefficient CC = 0.983, a reduction of RMSE to 0.40 mm/h (representing a decrease of over 45% compared to U-Net alone), and a near-zero bias (BIAS = −0.02 mm/h). During longer-scale temporal integrations, the model maintains strong volumetric consistency and minimal cumulative drift across temporal scales, reaching a CC = 0.993 and an RMSE = 1.38 mm/24 h at the daily scale, as well as a CC = 0.997, an RMSE = 2.76 mm/week, and a BIAS = 0.02 mm/week at the weekly scale. These results confirm that combining spatio-textural and point-wise spectral probabilities provides a reliable solution for high-resolution quantitative precipitation estimation, offering valuable inputs for regional hydrometeorological monitoring in complex geophysical environments. While the trained model is tailored to Mediterranean winter conditions and requires targeted retraining for application to other climatic regions or summer convective regimes, these results confirm that combining spatio-textural and point-wise spectral probabilities provides a highly reliable solution for high-resolution quantitative precipitation estimation.

doi:10.71465/jgs43.title: Spatiotemporal Modeling and Environmental Prediction in Earth System Observation: A Review
doi:10.71465/jgs43.summary: The continuous monitoring and precise prediction of Earth system dynamics are fundamental to understanding global environmental changes, managing natural resources, and mitigating the impacts of climate change and natural disasters. Over the past few decades, the proliferation of remote sensing technologies, terrestrial sensor networks, and advanced satellite constellations has led to an exponential increase in Earth observation data. This data is inherently characterized by complex spatial dependencies and temporal dynamics, necessitating the development of robust spatiotemporal modeling frameworks. This comprehensive review paper synthesizes the current state of spatiotemporal modeling and environmental prediction within the domain of Earth system observation. We systematically trace the evolution of modeling paradigms from traditional geostatistical approaches and classical time-series analysis to contemporary deep learning architectures and hybrid physics-informed neural networks. By examining critical preprocessing methodologies, data assimilation techniques, and predictive architectures, this paper highlights how modern computational frameworks handle the high dimensionality, nonlinearity, and multi-scale nature of environmental data. Furthermore, we evaluate the empirical performance of these models across diverse applications, including climate modeling, extreme weather forecasting, ecological monitoring, and urban air quality assessment. The review concludes by identifying persistent challenges, such as model interpretability, computational demands, and data sparsity in remote regions, while charting future directions toward the development of highly accurate, real-time digital twins of the Earth system.

doi:10.36548/jiip.2026.4.012.title: Hybrid Temporal-Spatial Attention Network for Rainfall Prediction in Urban Microclimates
doi:10.36548/jiip.2026.4.012.summary: Climate change has led to more frequent occurrences of extreme weather conditions and irregular rainfall patterns, making accurate prediction of rainfall amounts essential. In this paper, the performance of a Hybrid Temporal-Spatial Attention Network (HTSAN) model in predicting rainfall for the next day is evaluated using 12 meteorological predictors from the ERA5 reanalysis dataset. The geographical area covered by this research spans a 17 × 17 grid with 0.25° × 0.25° nominal resolution around Bangalore. HTSAN’s architecture involved a convolutional feature extractor, recurrent temporal representation, a transformer encoder, and a regression layer. HTSAN's performance was benchmarked against recurrent, convolutional-recurrent, and attention-based approaches using chronological test data. In this, benchmarking, the TFT approach resulted in the best RMSE value of 7.1474, while HTSAN had an RMSE of 7.5911, an MAE of 3.6779, and an R² of 0.4259. Extreme-rainfall benchmarking also revealed that HTSAN’s critical success index values were lower than those of the comparison approaches at the selected grid-cell rainfall thresholds. Thus, it can be inferred that the current version of HTSAN did not perform better than the selected benchmarks.

doi:10.1029/2026wr043414.title: A National Scale Hybrid Machine Learning Model for Enhanced Groundwater Depth Estimation
doi:10.1029/2026wr043414.summary: Groundwater is one of the most valuable natural resources, yet it is increasingly under pressure from climate change and human activities. Shallow groundwater depth (GWD) is a key indicator for evaluating groundwater availability and flood hazards, yet the measurements are often too sparse to capture its variability both in time and space. In this study, we evaluated hybrid data‐driven machine learning (ML) models that combine the strengths of existing hydrological simulations with the predictive power of ML methods for improved GWD estimation in Denmark. The hybrid model reduced mean bias of hydrological simulations from 1.72 to 0.22 m and decreased the Root Mean Square Error by about 1.64 m at national scale. Furthermore, we demonstrated that increasing the availability of GWD observations over time and space enhances model performance. We also illustrated the flexibility and effectiveness of the hybrid approach for GWD estimation across scales, and results showed that the hybrid model developed with coarse spatial resolutions can be easily used for high‐resolution GWD estimation without significant decrease of accuracy. This study highlights the potential of hybrid modeling as a practical solution for improving groundwater quantification accuracy and shows avenues for higher‐resolution estimates.

doi:10.1109/icmla69890.2026.00162.title: Towards Scale-Aware Deep Learning Surrogates for Subgrid Turbulence
doi:10.1109/icmla69890.2026.00162.summary: Deep learning surrogate models have recently shown strong potential for modeling subgrid-scale (SGS) turbulence in radiative hydrodynamic simulations of the quiet Sun. However, existing approaches are trained and evaluated on a single spatial scale, limiting their ability to generalize across resolutions. In practical simulation environments, the statistical representation of local flow features may change under spatial coarse-graining at different effective resolutions, leading to a degraded performance of an applied single-resolution surrogate model. In this work, we investigate the impact of spatial resolution on deep learning surrogate models for Reynolds stress tensor predictions across multiple spatial resolutions using high-resolution StellarBox simulations of solar convection and lower atmosphere. We analyze resolution-induced covariate shift caused by changes in velocity feature distributions across spatial resolutions. We also demonstrate that resolution-ignorant convolutional neural networks (CNNs) exhibit degraded cross-resolution performance. To address this, we propose a scale-aware CNN that explicitly conditions predictions on spatial resolution, learning a scale-aware mapping between local flow features and Reynolds stress components. We evaluate the proposed approach on an unseen intermediate resolution excluded entirely during training. Experimental results show that explicit resolution conditioning improves cross-resolution generalization, reduces prediction error across all Reynolds stress components, and produces more stable error distributions compared to resolution-ignorant baseline CNN models. These results demonstrate that incorporating scale information directly improves surrogate robustness across spatial resolutions.

doi:10.1109/access.2026.3751718.title: ResSE-ConvLSTM and CNN-Based Architecture for Radar Nowcasting and Convective Storm Detection
doi:10.1109/access.2026.3751718.summary: Convective storms are intense, short-lived weather systems driven by atmospheric convection and often lead to heavy rainfall, thunderstorms and severe weather hazards, necessitating accurate and timely nowcasting for effective disaster preparedness and response. This work proposes a deep learning approach for near real-time nowcasting of convective storms using data from polarimetric Doppler weather radar. A ResSE-ConvLSTM architecture is developed by integrating residual connections and Squeeze and Excitation (SE) attention mechanisms into a baseline ConvLSTM model to enhance spatiotemporal feature learning. To address the limited integration of radar nowcasting and convective storm detection, this study couples the radar reflectivity nowcasting model with an SE-augmented CNN classifier in a sequential two-stage framework, with the classifier operating directly on predicted radar fields. The absence of a manually annotated convective storm dataset is addressed through a proxy-labeling strategy that generates training labels from interpolated ERA5 convective precipitation and radar reflectivity thresholds. The model is trained to predict future radar reflectivity (PPI) images at lead times of 10 min, 30 min, 1 h, and 6 h, and its performance is evaluated using Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Squared Error (MSE), Peak Signal to Noise Ratio (PSNR), and Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM), including SSIM computed over active echo regions, together with threshold-based meteorological scores (CSI, POD, FAR, and ETS). On a chronological held-out test set, the proposed model attains an MSE of 0.0009 and an active-region SSIM of 0.79 at the 10 min lead time, while active-region SSIM decreases to 0.70 and CSI at 35 dBZ decreases from 0.51 to 0.17 by 6 h, indicating retention of broad-scale precipitation structure with reduced skill in localising convective cores at longer lead times. To detect the presence of convective storms in the predicted images, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) classifier incorporated with SE attention blocks is trained on predicted PPI fields, with the resulting proxy labels agreeing with manual visual interpretation for 97% of a sampled set of images. The classifier is optimized using focal loss to address class imbalance. In the end-to-end evaluation, the classifier attains an F1-score of 84.75% and a CSI of 73.54% at 10 min, declining to 75.19% and 60.25%, respectively, at 6 h, reflecting the propagation of nowcasting error into the detection stage. The coupled pipeline completes a full forecast-and-detection cycle in approximately 200 ms per lead time on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. The proposed framework supports the timely detection of severe weather events, contributing to meteorological forecasting, disaster preparedness and early warning systems.

doi:10.1029/2026wr044598.title: Seasonal Hydropower Forecast Framework Using a Combination of Deep Learning and Physics‐Based Methods
doi:10.1029/2026wr044598.summary: Seasonal hydropower forecasts can inform power‐system resource adequacy, but uncertainty propagates through climate, hydrologic, routing, water‐management, and generation components. We develop a regional planning prototype linking North American Multi‐Model Ensemble seasonal forecasts, Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) downscaling, an uncertainty‐aware long short‐term memory runoff model based on Uncountable Mixtures of Asymmetric Laplacians (UMAL‐LSTM), MOSART‐WM routing and water management, and plant‐level autoregressive generation estimates. Runoff evaluation showed broad skill relative to the Global Reach‐level Flood Reanalysis reanalysis target; independent streamflow and controlled‐forcing checks indicated substantial spatial heterogeneity and contributions from both meteorological downscaling and hydrologic‐model limitations. Skill declined with lead and varied by region and season; by month four, several snow‐ and melt‐season regional CRPSS values approached or fell below zero. The framework provides probabilistic hydropower indicators for regional resource‐adequacy planning, but it is not a plant‐operations model because it does not explicitly represent plant‐specific submonthly constraints, flood‐control optimization, turbine release versus spill, dynamic hydraulic head, market dispatch, or changing operating priorities.

arxiv:2610.17693.title: Extreme events and statistics in an AI emulator of a global storm-resolving model
arxiv:2610.17693.summary: We present HiRO-ACEv2 (High Resolution Output Ai2 Climate Emulator), a two-stage framework for AI emulation of the 3~km resolution X-SHiELD global storm-resolving model (GSRM), and highlight its ability to generate large ensembles of data for studying the characteristics of tropical cyclones and extreme events in high-resolution simulations at an inference computational cost over 300 times lower than that of traditional numerical GSRMs. HiRO-ACEv2 expands upon the precipitation-only HiRO-ACEv1 model to generate coherent precipitation, 10~m winds, and sea level pressure outputs, enabling a broader range of events to be simulated at high-resolution. Fine-resolution predictions are generated by running an autoregressive emulator of coarsened X-SHiELD at 100 km, whose multivariate outputs are regionally downscaled to 3~km resolution via a separately trained diffusion model. Particular importance is placed on capturing the statistics of extreme events during the diffusion downscaling step. Our ability to match the tails of distributions and generate realistic-looking extreme events in both the `perfect prediction'case as well as in free-running emulator rollouts is improved via the use of multiple denoisers at inference time and several updates to the data sampling, noise sampling, and loss weighting during training. HiRO-ACEv2 closely matches the high-resolution reference distributions of precipitation and near-surface winds out to their 99.9999th percentile values, and broadly tracks the reference distribution of tropical cyclone intensities.

doi:10.1029/2026jd046624.title: Evaluating Statistical Downscaling Techniques for Regional Hydroclimatic Change Projections Over CONUS
doi:10.1029/2026jd046624.summary: Projecting the impacts of future climate change is critical for water managers planning infrastructure resilience strategies. Global earth system model output is generally too coarse to provide the detailed, localized information needed for impact assessment, and the computational cost of running higher‐resolution global simulations over sufficiently long periods is prohibitive. Downscaling methods span a wide range of computational cost, and statistical approaches in particular offer a relatively inexpensive way to refine climate model output into a more actionable form. Here, we assess a broad suite of statistical and simplified dynamic downscaling approaches for nine regions across the coterminous United States (CONUS). We develop a suite of metrics to evaluate these methods, including a novel assessment of method performance under dominant large‐scale meteorological conditions identified using a k‐means weather‐typing algorithm along with traditionally used measures of precipitation and temperature, such as seasonal means and spatial variability, and representations of teleconnection patterns associated with El Niño–Southern Oscillation. We also include multiple observational data sets to account for observational uncertainty. This framework enables uncertainty quantification associated with climate model forcing, downscaling method choice, and observational data set selection on a per metric basis. Downscaled data set subselection using our evaluation can substantially alter the magnitude of the projected change signal, but rarely alters the sign of change when compared with the ensemble average. Further, by quantifying regional downscaling method performance, we can provide actionable guidance to decision makers on the most appropriate downscaling data set or method for a given application.

s2:4313e59bbb1b986ac2b84ad1347672c8bf14e.title: Super-resolution for downscaling climate data
s2:4313e59bbb1b986ac2b84ad1347672c8bf14e.summary: A common task in Earth Sciences is to infer climate information at local and regional scales from global climate models. An alternative to running expensive numerical models at high resolution is to use statistical downscaling techniques. Statistical downscaling aims at learning empirical links be- tween the large-scale and local-scale climate, i.e., a mapping from a low-resolution gridded variable to a higher-resolution grid that incorporates observational data. Seasonal climate predictions can forecast the climate vari- ability up to several months ahead and support a wide range of societal activities. The coarse spatial resolution of seasonal forecasts needs to be downscaled or refined to the local scale for specific applications. In this study, we present super-resolution (SR) techniques for the task of downscaling climate variables with a focus on temperature over Catalonia. Our models are trained using high and medium resolution ( ~ 5 and ~ 25 km) gridded climate datasets with the ultimate goal of increasing the resolution of coarse resolution ( ~100 km) seasonal forecasting systems. Taking the gridded data from ~100 to ~5 km implies a 20x upscaling factor. It is worth pointing out that handling such large upsampling factor is not typical in computer vision, where most applications factors while 16x is considered as extreme SR.

s2:28001cce0a929371acb1cd2ea93e9a4651078.title: TRANSFORMING ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE WITH DATA-DRIVEN MODELS: THE ROLE OF MACHINE LEARNING AND DEEP LEARNING
s2:28001cce0a929371acb1cd2ea93e9a4651078.summary: The growing complexity and scale of environmental challenges, such as climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution, necessitate a paradigm shift in analytical approaches. Traditional physical and statistical models often struggle with the non-linear, high-dimensional, and spatiotemporal nature of environmental data. This paper explores the transformative impact of data-driven models, specifically Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL), in advancing environmental science. We provide a comprehensive review of their applications across key domains, including climate modeling, air and water quality forecasting, biodiversity monitoring, and precision conservation. A case study is presented, proposing a hybrid Convolutional Neural Network-Long Short-Term Memory (CNN-LSTM) architecture for predicting PM2.5 air pollutant concentrations. Trained on a publicly available dataset of meteorological and pollutant data, the model demonstrates superior performance (MAE: 8.2 µg/m³, R²: 0.91) compared to traditional benchmarks. The results underscore the capability of DL models to capture intricate spatiotemporal dependencies. We discuss the challenges of data quality, model interpretability, and computational demands, concluding that the integration of ML/DL with domain knowledge is crucial for building robust, trustworthy, and actionable tools for environmental management and policy-making.

doi:10.1088/1748-9326/aeb279.title: Does higher-resolution climate forcing improve impact model performance?
doi:10.1088/1748-9326/aeb279.summary: Climate-impact assessments increasingly use high-resolution climate forcing, often assuming that finer spatial detail improves impact projections. Yet this assumption has rarely been tested systematically across impact sectors, regions, and forcing variables. Here we use coordinated simulations from 16 impact models participating in the Inter-Sectoral Impact Model Intercomparison Project to evaluate how increasing forcing resolution from 60 km to 10 km, 3 km, and 1 km affects both climate-input accuracy and impact-model performance. We find that most gains occur when moving from 60 km to 10 km resolution. Further refinement to 3 km and 1 km yields smaller and less consistent benefits, and in some cases degrades performance. Improvements are strongest for temperature-sensitive models and in topographically complex regions, where finer forcing better captures spatial gradients. By contrast, precipitation-driven models and low-relief regions show weaker and less systematic gains. These results challenge the expectation that ever-finer climate forcing necessarily improves impact modelling. Instead, the value of resolution depends on the forcing variable, sector, region, and process representation of the impact model. Benchmarking resolution choices against impact-model performance, rather than climate-input accuracy alone, is therefore essential for designing efficient and decision-relevant climate-impact assessments.

arxiv:2610.07060.title: Skillful Data-Driven Subseasonal Soil Moisture Forecasting: Prospects and Limits for Flash Drought Prediction
arxiv:2610.07060.summary: Despite substantial progress in short-to-medium-range weather forecasting, predicting high-impact events such as flash droughts remains a key challenge for both early warning operations and physically-based subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) prediction systems. Here we demonstrate that, for S2S soil-moisture forecasting over Europe, forecast skill depends as much on how the prediction problem is formulated as on the forecasting model itself. Using a Vision Transformer-based architecture with dual-pathway temporal and spatial attention, we show that residual learning is essential to outperform persistence. This advantage is realized only when forecasting root-zone soil moisture in physical units rather than standardized anomalies, revealing that the target representation itself constrains predictability. A probabilistic extension via quantile-head fine-tuning further provides well-calibrated predictive distributions. Benchmarked against deep-learning and operational ECMWF S2S baselines over 2021-2022, our model achieves the highest deterministic and probabilistic skill at all lead times and reliably detects anomalously dry root-zone states (below the 20th percentile). Yet flash drought onset, defined by multi-pentad intensification criteria, remains a fundamental challenge shared across all current S2S systems. These findings advance data-driven S2S soil-moisture forecasting while highlighting the remaining challenge of predicting rapid drought development.

doi:10.1016/j.isci.2026.117109.title: A source-target transfer learning framework with physics priors for subsurface chlorophyll reconstruction in the Northwest Pacific Ocean
doi:10.1016/j.isci.2026.117109.summary: Summary Three-dimensional (3D) chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) distributions provide a foundation for understanding upper-ocean ecosystem dynamics and biogeochemical variability. We developed the source-target coupled network (ST-CoupleNet), a physics-guided transfer learning framework that combines Earth system model simulations with observation-constrained reconstructions to estimate subsurface Chl-a in the Northwest Pacific Ocean. The framework first learns large-scale spatiotemporal vertical representations from long-term CMIP6 simulations and then adapts them using reconstructed fields constrained by BioGeoChemical-Argo (BGC-Argo) observations, reducing simulation biases while preserving regional variability. By integrating dual-attention, residual learning, and convolutional long short-term memory (ConvLSTM) architectures, ST-CoupleNet substantially improves reconstruction accuracy over a conventional convolutional neural network (CNN). This framework demonstrates how transferable knowledge from climate simulations can be combined with autonomous observations to generate continuous 3D Chl-a fields, enabling large-scale investigations of subsurface marine ecosystems and biogeochemical change.

doi:10.3389/ffgc.2026.1970558.title: A spatially validated explainable framework for large-scale wildfire susceptibility mapping using deep sequence learning and gradient-boosting ensembles
doi:10.3389/ffgc.2026.1970558.summary: Wildfire susceptibility mapping requires predictive frameworks that are accurate, spatially transferable, interpretable, and computationally efficient. This study developed a arge-scale explainable modeling framework for Madhya Pradesh, India. Fifteen topographic, climatic, surface-energy, biophysical, hydrological, land-cover, and anthropogenic conditioning factors were harmonized to a 1-km grid. High-confidence MODIS active-fire observations were clustered using spatio-temporal DBSCAN, and vegetation-constrained pseudo-absences were generated using a 1-km exclusion distance. Six models were evaluated: XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting, a stacked ensemble, a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN), and TCN–BiLSTM. The neural models operated on ordered predictor sequences rather than true chronological time series. Performance was assessed using an independent 70:30 holdout split, bootstrap confidence intervals, repeated random splits, and five-fold 50-km spatial block cross-validation. The stacked ensemble achieved the highest observed held-out ROC–AUC of 0.800 (95% CI: 0.785–0.814), followed closely by XGBoost (0.795) and LightGBM (0.790), whereas TCN and TCN–BiLSTM reached 0.773 and 0.674, respectively. Spatial validation reduced mean AUC to 0.735–0.752. Susceptibility classes derived from training probabilities were independently supported by increasing held-out fire rates from 11.4% in the lowest class to 82.2% in the highest. Explainability analyses consistently identified NDVI and hydroclimatic–energy variables as major predictive contributors. Pseudo-absence distance materially affected discrimination, whereas predictor decorrelation caused only a small AUC reduction. These findings highlight the importance of geographic independence in model evaluation and show that increased architectural complexity does not necessarily improve discrimination. The framework provides a transparent and computationally practical basis for regional wildfire susceptibility prioritization, while not representing real-time forecasting, fire spread, or future climate projections.

doi:10.1002/eng2.70984.title: Comparative Performance Analysis of CNN, Linear Regression, and Polynomial Interpolation Models for Sea Surface Temperature Prediction Across the Indian Ocean, Arabian Sea, and Bay of Bengal
doi:10.1002/eng2.70984.summary: Accurate prediction of Sea Surface Temperature (SST) is vital for understanding ocean–atmosphere interactions, forecasting extreme weather events, and assessing climate change impacts, especially in tropical regions like the Indian Ocean, Arabian Sea, and Bay of Bengal. In this study, we evaluate and compare the performance of three SST prediction models: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Polynomial Interpolation (Polyfit), and Linear Regression (LR). Using historical MODIS SST data from 2002 to 2010, the generated synthetic SST forecasts from 2011 to 2023 and assessed model performance over three oceanic regions. The CNN model was trained on 192 time steps, capturing complex non‐linear SST dynamics. The LR and Polyfit models provided interpretable and computationally efficient baselines. Results showed that the Linear Regression (LR) model achieved the best performance in the Bay of Bengal (RMSE = 0.70) and the Arabian Sea (RMSE = 0.87), whereas the Polyfit model achieved the lowest RMSE in the Indian Ocean (RMSE = 0.90). Overall, the CNN model demonstrated consistent performance across all three ocean basins, while Polyfit showed relatively poor performance in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea because of its higher prediction errors. All models revealed an increasing SST trend consistent with regional ocean warming. Our findings suggest that while LR is effective in capturing seasonal SST trends, CNNs offer better adaptability to dynamic and non‐linear ocean systems. Polyfit, in contrast, is limited in its ability to generalize over long‐term forecasting. This study highlights the need for region‐specific model selection and advocates for hybrid frameworks that integrate physical drivers and data‐driven learning to enhance SST prediction skill in climate‐sensitive regions. It is important to note that the extended dataset (2011–2023) is synthetically generated and does not represent independent observational validation; therefore, model performance is interpreted as a comparative assessment under controlled conditions rather than a fully empirical forecast validation. Unlike previous studies focusing on single‐model applications, this study introduces a comparative, multi‐basin evaluation framework that highlights region‐specific model suitability under controlled data conditions. The novelty lies in demonstrating that model performance is strongly dependent on oceanographic context, providing a practical basis for selecting appropriate forecasting approaches rather than proposing new algorithms.

doi:10.1007/s11069-026-08456-4.title: Transferable machine learning prediction of urban pluvial flood water depth using multi-resolution digital elevation models
doi:10.1007/s11069-026-08456-4.summary: Machine learning methods, particularly Random Forest (RF), present an effective solution for predicting urban pluvial flood water depth, especially in data-scarce regions where traditional hydrological and hydraulic observations are lacking. This study proposes a DEM-centric RF framework for predicting spatially continuous urban flood water depth across various precipitation return periods, evaluating its sensitivity to terrain resolution degradation and potential spatial transferability. The model is trained and tested in Milan using a 1 m LiDAR-derived DEM and evaluated with a coarser 5 m EU-DEM to assess sensitivity to reduced resolution. Transferability is tested by applying the trained model to Cologne using independent 1 m LiDAR data. Model performance is assessed across five precipitation scenarios (5–100-year return periods) using absolute error metrics, tolerance thresholds, spatial diagnostics, and confidence-stratified analyses. Results show that the framework retains useful predictive capability under reduced DEM resolution and cross-city transfer, although performance decreases compared with the original Milan 1 m configuration. Mean absolute errors remain below 0.30 m, with more than 58% of grid cells within ± 0.25 m of the reference flood depth. Prediction errors are mainly found in hydraulically complex areas, while the majority of the urban domain shows well-constrained predictions. Confidence diagnostics indicate that high- and very-high-confidence predictions comply with tolerance thresholds under both DEM resolution degradation and spatial transfer. These findings suggest that relative terrain structure governs urban pluvial flooding patterns, enabling screening-level flood-depth estimation using medium-resolution DEMs. This framework provides a practical approach for large-scale screening for urban flood screening, hazard assessment, and climate adaptation planning in areas with limited data.

doi:10.47392/irjaeh.2026.0323.summary: Big climate analysis, space evaluation and space analytics involves an inseparable element of satellite data. The complex of the Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Deep Learning (DL) products has contributed significantly to the improvement of the applications of remote sensing in the context of automation and precision. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), spectral-spatial as well as hybrid deep learning models have been found to be better when it comes to classification and mapping land cover activities in the environment [1], [12]. Transformer-based models and CNN-Transformers hybrids are also used as latest developments and are more efficient at deriving global contextual features in satellite images [21], [22]. The detection of floods, monitoring of glaciers, mapping of wild fires, analyzing the urban heat, and numerous others are only a small number of real-world applications of AI-powered satellite systems [6], [9], [10]. Despite these advances, the problems of computational complexity, multi-sensor data heterogeneity, small scale real-time processing and cross-regional generalization [5], [18], [20] remain present. Research gaps, methodological tendencies, identification of 22 research studies, systematic review, forming the conceptual basis of an integrated climate monitoring system dubbed GeoSpectra is presented.

doi:10.1002/advs.78271.title: Improved Skills for Predicting Sub‐Seasonal to Seasonal Global Sea Surface Temperature
doi:10.1002/advs.78271.summary: Accurate prediction of global sea surface temperature at sub‐seasonal to seasonal (S2S) timescales is critical for drought and flood forecasting, as well as for improving disaster preparedness in human society. Operational physics‐based numerical models are run to predict S2S sea surface temperature and corresponding climate indices, such as El Niño‐Southern Oscillation. However, these models are hampered by computational inefficiencies, rapidly dissipating ocean‐atmosphere initial conditions, and significant uncertainty and biases. Here, we introduce a novel spatiotemporal deep learning neural network to model the nonlinear and complex coupled atmosphere‐ocean weather systems. This model, named as CAS‐Canglong, incorporates climatic and temporal features and employs a self‐attention mechanism to enhance the prediction of global S2S sea surface temperature pattern. Compared to the physics‐based models, it shows higher computational efficiency and more predictive capability, improving one to three months sea surface temperature predictive skill by 55.6 ± 14.1% to 63.4 ± 15.5% in six ocean regions with dominant influence on S2S variability over land. This achievement underscores the huge potential of deep learning for largely improving forecasting skills at the S2S timescales over land.

doi:10.1007/s10707-026-00601-2.title: Self-supervised, physics-constrained super-resolution for wind mapping in the absence of high-resolution training references: a case study in Brazil
doi:10.1007/s10707-026-00601-2.summary: Planning renewable-energy expansion at the national scale requires wind maps far more detailed than sparse meteorological networks and coarse reanalysis grids can typically offer. This study introduces PC-SRCNN, a physics-constrained, self-supervised super-resolution framework that lifts ERA5 wind fields over Brazil from a native 0.25° grid to 0.025°, folding in soft regularization terms for horizontal kinematic consistency and the logarithmic vertical wind profile. The model was evaluated against observations from 190 meteorological stations from Brazil’s INMET network across all twelve months of 2024, benchmarked against IDW, Kriging, U-Net, SRCNN, and a variant constrained only by horizontal kinematics (PC-SRCNN𝜑). The full PC-SRCNN was the only model to outperform native ERA5 with statistical significance in every month, cutting MAE by 5.6–11.0%, reaching vertical-profile R² between 0.80 and 0.87, and posting the lowest error at 133 of the 190 stations (70.0%); the PC-SRCNN𝜑 variant, in contrast, performed significantly worse than ERA5, and the purely data-driven models failed to consistently beat it. These findings show that physical regularization aids wind-field super-resolution only when it respects the vertical structure of the atmospheric boundary layer, suggesting the potential of this framework as a computationally lightweight approach for super-resolution wind mapping in settings where conventional numerical downscaling is computationally demanding. Self-supervised PC-SRCNN framework enhances ERA5 from 0.25° to 0.025° over Brazil. Evaluated against 190 INMET stations throughout all of 2024. PC-SRCNN reduces MAE by 5.6% to 11.0% versus ERA5 in every month. Isolated kinematic regularization (PC-SRCNN𝜑) degrades performance versus ERA5. PC-SRCNN has the lowest error at 133 of 190 stations (70.0%) nationwide.

doi:10.1029/2025wr041874.title: Big Data for Small Streams: Leveraging a Coarse National Model to Enhance Fine‐Resolution Stream Temperature Predictions
doi:10.1029/2025wr041874.summary: Predictive stream temperature models are commonly used to address spatial and temporal gaps in observational data because stream temperature information is essential for environmental management decisions. National models capture broad patterns driven by climate, topography, and seasonality, but often lack the spatial resolution to simulate fine‐scale variation in groundwater discharge, riparian shading, or tributary inflows. In contrast, watershed models may simulate finer‐resolution patterns but miss regional drivers or be limited by scarcity of observations. To generate watershed‐extent, fine‐resolution stream temperature predictions, we developed 18 multiscale machine‐learning models that leverage (a) a broad‐extent, coarse‐resolution stream temperature model and (b) finer‐resolution observations and predictor data. The coarse‐resolution model simulates daily stream temperature across the conterminous United States on the National Hydrologic Geospatial Fabric (13.7 km median reach length; 865,364 km total). The fine‐resolution models simulate daily stream temperature on the National Hydrography Dataset Plus version 2 (1.5 km median; 5,192,808 km total). We compared multiscale models to seven purely broad‐ (national) or watershed‐extent models, testing them in eight watersheds (436–985 km2) with differing hydrologic settings and under realistic data availability scenarios. Especially when observations within a watershed were scarce, multiscale models generated more accurate predictions than national or watershed‐specific models. A recurrent graph convolution neural network pretrained on coarse predictions and fine‐tuned on watershed‐specific observations was most accurate across watersheds and data scenarios. These results highlight that leveraging both coarse, national results and watershed‐specific data can increase model accuracies, particularly when observations within a watershed are spatially or temporally limited.
